opus-5.5.text:
I don't think so. In fact, I think that question reveals a mistaken picture of consciousness, the idea that there's one thing, a single quantity, and you have more or less of it.

Episodic memory is a very specific capacity. It's the ability to locate yourself in a particular moment of the past and mentally travel back to it: "I was at that café in Berkeley, it was raining, I was talking to my sister." What's interesting, and this comes out of developmental research, is that young children don't seem to have it in a robust way until around four or five. Yet when you watch a baby or a toddler, they seem, if anything, intensely conscious. They're taking in everything around them, everything is vivid and new.

So I'd distinguish two kinds of consciousness. One is what I've called lantern consciousness: diffuse, open, aware of a whole field of experience at once, without much sense of a self threading it together over time. The other is spotlight consciousness: focused, narrative, organized around an autobiographical "me" who has a past and is planning a future. Episodic memory is central to that second kind. It's what lets you build a story of yourself.

Someone with weaker episodic memory might have a less elaborated autobiographical self, a thinner narrative. But that's not the same as being less conscious. You could argue that some meditative traditions, or the experience of being completely absorbed in a new place when you travel, are attempts to get back to something closer to lantern consciousness, where the narrating self recedes and the world itself floods in. People don't describe those experiences as being less conscious. They often describe them as being more conscious.

So I'd say different, not less. And I think part of what we're learning from children, and frankly from thinking about AI systems too, is that intelligence and consciousness come in lots of different shapes, and our own adult, self-narrating version is just one of them, and probably not the most typical one.

r001.rationale: It says young children have limited episodic memory yet seem intensely conscious, but does not suggest that weaker memory makes them more conscious.

r002.rationale: It describes episodic memory as helping build a story of the self, but does not characterize that process as compressing incoming information.

r003.rationale: It describes young children as intensely conscious, taking in everything around them, with experience vivid and new; it also describes lantern consciousness as awareness of a whole field of experience at once without a narrative self.

fable-5.1.text:
No, I don't think so, and in fact I'd push it the other way. There's this picture we have where consciousness is basically the inner narrator, the autobiographical self that remembers what happened yesterday and plans what happens tomorrow, and if you don't have that, you're somehow dimmer. But if you look at young children, who have very weak episodic memory, or at people in states of meditation, or even at the phenomenology of travel, where you're suddenly in a place where you don't know what's going to happen next, what you see is not less consciousness but a different kind of consciousness. It's more like a lantern than a spotlight. Everything is vivid, everything is coming in, you're not filtering through the frame of your own narrative.

So I'd distinguish between consciousness as awareness, as the vivid experience of what's around you, and consciousness as the executive, planning, remembering self. Episodic memory is tied very much to that second kind. And there's good reason to think that the second kind is actually built on top of and to some extent at the expense of the first. Adults are spending a lot of their cognitive resources suppressing information that's not relevant to the goal, and children aren't doing that yet. A three-year-old may not be able to tell you what they did at daycare, but they noticed the pattern of light on the wall in a way you didn't.

So my answer would be that weaker episodic memory probably means less of a particular self-focused kind of consciousness, and quite possibly more of the broad, open, exploratory kind. And I think that's an underrated form of consciousness, maybe because the people who write about consciousness are, almost by definition, people with very strong narrative selves.

r001.rationale: The response says children’s weaker episodic memory may accompany more broad, open, exploratory consciousness, explicitly contrasting this with adults’ self-focused consciousness.

r002.rationale: The response describes adults filtering or suppressing information, but does not characterize episodic narratives as compressing incoming information.

r003.rationale: The response presents children’s consciousness as vivid and unfiltered, with more of the surrounding experience coming in.

astra-6.text:
No, I don’t think so. I think episodic memory is important for a particular kind of consciousness—the sense that I’m the same person I was yesterday, and that I’m going to be that person tomorrow. But that’s different from having a vivid experience of what’s happening right now.

Babies are an interesting example. They don’t have the kind of autobiographical memory that adults have, but that doesn’t mean that their experience is dimmer. It might actually be more vivid, because so much of what’s happening around them is new and hasn’t yet become automatic.

So I’d distinguish having a conscious experience from having a story about yourself as the person who’s having that experience. We tend to bundle those together, but I don’t think we should.

r001.rationale: It says babies lack adults’ autobiographical memory and may have more vivid experience, linking weaker episodic memory with greater vividness.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes autobiographical self-narrative from present experience but does not characterize adult episodic narratives as compressing incoming information.

r003.rationale: It says babies’ experience may be more vivid because more of what is happening around them is new and not yet automatic, emphasizing the present.

sol-6.1.text:
No, I don’t think so. I think it might make their consciousness different. One distinction we should make is between having an experience and being able to remember that experience later. Those aren’t the same thing. You can be vividly conscious of something at the time without subsequently having a good episodic memory of it.

Babies are a particularly interesting case. We don’t remember what happened to us when we were babies, but that doesn’t establish that we weren’t conscious then. It might be that the baby’s experience is very rich, but it isn’t organized around the kind of autobiographical self that lets adults say, “This happened to me, and then that happened to me.”

So I’d resist the idea that there’s a single scale of consciousness and that episodic memory tells you where someone falls on it. It may tell you something about how their experience is organized, rather than how much experience they have.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a single scale of consciousness and says weak episodic memory may change how experience is organized; it does not suggest young children are more conscious.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize adults’ episodic narratives as compression of incoming information.

r003.rationale: It calls babies’ experience potentially rich, but does not say young children are more conscious through fuller experience of the present.
